item.title: My Catastrophizing Was a Catastrophe I Learned to Stop
item.description:
Catastrophizing

My Catastrophizing Was a Catastrophe I Learned to Stop

Personal Perspective: Living with fear is really no way to live.

Posted August 20, 2026

Here it is again. Life as catastrophe. The drumbeat of terrors. What if I never publish another novel? What if I or a loved one succumbs to a devastating disease? What if I give a reading and no one shows up? What if all our money vanishes and we are left to live on the street?

The terrors, like in this local Halloween decoration, seem really real.
Source: Caroline Leavitt

It's OK to snicker here, except all of this feels so real to me. All of it keeps me up at night, and oh, OK, in the daytime, too.

But shaking this off is hard. One bit of doom thinking jumpstarts all other catastrophic thinking about what could happen. And for me, who grew up on catastrophe, it’s like cling wrap.

And for me, it’s learned behavior I want to unlearn.

Growing up, catastrophizing was a way of life taught by my mom and my sister. They believed if you thought about the absolute worst thing happening, you’d be prepared for it. This had to do with terrifying fears about gym class, where I’d be made to leap up onto parallel bars, the same bars that sent another girl to the ER the week before. When I got sick with lung infections, which happened a lot, there was always talk in my house that I was near death. Worse, when I was healthy, catastrophizing carried warnings. Don’t go outside because it’s too cold/too hot/too humid. You know how you get, which really meant: You know what could happen and it won’t be good. The message was clear: Pay attention to the bad, because it can happen again, and it probably will.

But more distressingly, my mom and sister loved disaster. "Send me books where someone is really sick," my sister used to urge. My mother insisted that there was a curse on the Leavitt woman, that we all were destined to have hard, unhappy lives, and though it pains me to say this, every time there was, she sort of smiled. She seemed to love me more.

I was able to shake a lot of it by being Pollyanna about life. No, no, the worst thing wouldn’t happen. The best might! My mother scoffed. My sister ridiculed me. They both showed me what they thought was proof that catastrophe always happened to me:

My first husband cheated on me for five years and then booted me out of our home. My mother told me it would get worse: He’d be snapped right up, and I’d be alone.

Next, my young and healthy fiancé dropped dead in my arms two weeks before our wedding. I worried so much about this happening again that when years later I married my now husband, I cried through the ceremony, terrified, but all that happened was we were married!

I lost our baby at four and a half months of pregnancy. My sister insisted I was too old, but I got pregnant again six months later.

Next, we had a beautiful, healthy baby boy, and I became critically ill with a blood disorder and was expected to die. I had to go back to a hematologist every week for four years, and on year five, I stopped because all these appointments made me believe that something bad was going to happen. And nothing did.

article continues after advertisement

Of course, I know all of those things could have gotten worse and more painful. Of course, I fought my worries. But instead, something else happened. Something good.

Leaving my first husband and our Pittsburgh home brought me to Manhattan and a life where I was happier than I had ever been before.

Although it took me years to get over the shock of my fiancé’s death, I learned what a loving relationship really looked and felt like, and I was able to recreate it with my now husband.

Yes, we lost a baby, but now we have the best, most amazing son we ever could have had.

And yes, I was critically ill, but that made me realize how nothing mattered—not all the things I worried or catastrophized about—except for love, and that was what life was all about. That, and living in the moment more, in realizing that all worry does is create more worry.

Sometime worries are tiny, like these fake hands.
Source: Caroline Leavitt

Actually, my son gave me the key to catastrophizing. I was worried about staying alone in our home while Jeff was working in Norway. What if someone broke in, I worried? What if the heat went out? My son patiently answered each fear. The locks were sound. The police were close. I lived in a city and could call a plumber or go to a friend's. “What if there are ghosts?” I asked him, and I was half serious, or at least my imagination was. My son sighed. “Did that ever happen before to you?” he asked. “Is there any reason why it would happen now?”

There wasn’t, and it didn’t. I know that, of course, bad things happen that we can’t control. But when you dwell on the dark fears, you stay in the dark fears, even when all you need to do is find and focus on that brief blink of light that’s beckoning you a little further along the way.

item.title: Why Emotional Regulation Is Harm Prevention
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Why Emotional Regulation Is Harm Prevention

Untaught emotional skills are at the root of many modern crises.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional regulation is a critical harm prevention skill, not just a "soft skill."
  • Naming emotions is the first step toward healthier, intentional responses.
  • Teaching emotional regulation is essential for resilient relationships and safer societies.

Years ago, I had a client, 26 years young, who sat across from me clenching his jaw and his fists and told me it was taking every ounce of strength he could muster to refrain from trashing my office. I could see, in his face and hands especially, that he meant it. The anger toward his job, at his partner, and at his parents had been building for months, and it felt like it was about to come out of him whether he wanted it to or not. Nobody had ever taught him what to do with it, not his parents or coaches, and not a single teacher.

I repeatedly see emotional regulation categorized as a "soft skill," something nice to have alongside the "real work." But it is often the key difference between chaos, violence, and calamity, and thriving, health, and connection.

Emotion is one of the fastest forces in us. It registers in thousandths of a second (LeDoux, 2000), whereas thought often takes a quarter to half a second to catch up (Kent & Wittmann, 2021). By the time we've formed a coherent thought about what we're feeling, the feeling likely already ran the show (LeDoux, 2000). This is not a metaphor; it’s the nervous system doing what it has evolved to do. E(motion), the word itself, comes from the Latin emovere, meaning “to move out” or “to move.” Emotion is thus quite literally connected to movement.

Emotions are also crucial data. They reveal that what is happening matters: danger, a loss, an injustice, a disconnection you haven't named yet. This is why I've referred to it as an inner GPS in an earlier post. It orients before your thinking mind can catch up.

And emotions are also how we actually connect with each other, most of the time, before a single word is said. You know fear when you see it in someone's face. You know loneliness in the way a person pulls back in a social setting. You know anger in a jaw, a fist, a voice gone flat. Words come later, and often they come to explain what the body already gave away. Emotions are thus the real language of relationship (and why the relational therapy I practice is called emotionally focused). Strong, healthy relationships also effectively help us manage overwhelming emotions.

So why are we so bad at managing our emotions? Because we were raised in a culture that treats emotion like a problem to manage rather than essential information. Calm down. Toughen up. Get over it. Don't cry. Don't be so sensitive. Don't make this awkward. We've been taught for generations that the feeling itself is the malfunction, not what happens when one has not learned what to do with it.

Here's what I tell clients, and what I wish someone had told the client above before he ended up in my office in that state: Ignored emotion doesn't go away. It gets louder. It bleeds out sideways, often forcibly projected into the wrong relationship, the wrong moment, and/or the wrong place. And one cannot regulate what they were never taught to recognize in the first place.

Naming what you feel is a first step. Naming your anger can already make you a little less angry (Lieberman et al., 2007). Awareness already gets you past the starting line. Regulation is the work you do after that (the part nobody handed my aforementioned client a map for him to learn). This distinction matters because emotional regulation is ultimately about learning to intentionally choose your response to your emotion instead of allowing it to overtake you before you have a say.

article continues after advertisement

Effective, intentional emotion regulation is crime prevention. A 2026 meta-analysis in Aggressive Behavior (Smith et al., 2026) found that people who can stay aware of and accept difficult emotions, rather than suppress them, show meaningfully lower rates of reactive aggression, the kind that erupts unplanned. Likewise, Wang and Amin (2026) found that emotional dysregulation, along with the impulsivity and chronic stress it tends to travel with, explained close to 44 percent of the variance in violent behavior in a large adult sample. This suggests that a substantial portion of aggressive behavior is rooted in a lack of effective emotional regulation and coping skills.

The implications go beyond individual outbursts. Violence, greed, exploitation, sexual violence, dehumanization (the way conflict escalates past the point anyone intended): So much of what goes wrong in the world traces back, at least in part, to emotional dysregulation. That's not the same as saying emotions cause these things, or that regulation explains away responsibility for them. It means our capacity to tolerate the hard stuff—fear, shame, envy, helplessness, frustration—shapes what we do with power and conflict, and how we treat the people we're responsible for.

Someone who can't tolerate shame may attack the nearest available target just to escape it. Someone who can't tolerate helplessness may try to control everything within reach. Someone who cannot tolerate fear may turn another into an enemy. Multiply that across a family, an organization, a country, and regulation stops being a private therapeutic skill. It is a major, global public health issue.

It's also addiction prevention. Emotion dysregulation is consistently tied to greater substance use, and strengthening that regulation may be one of the more reliable levers for reducing it (Weiss et al., 2022). This tracks with what I see in this office. People rarely pick up a substance because they enjoy chaos. They pick it up because it's the fastest exit available from a feeling they never learned to sit with and manage.

It's suicide prevention too. A 2024 systematic review in Healthcare (Rogante et al., 2024) found emotion dysregulation to be one of the most consistent predictors of suicidal ideation. Carvalho and colleagues (2023) found the inverse holds as well: Adaptive emotion regulation acted as a protective factor, lowering suicide risk even in traumatized young people. Regulation isn't only about staying composed; it's often what's between someone and the worst outcome imaginable.

article continues after advertisement

And it travels. Buckholdt, Parra, and Jobe-Shields (2013) found that when caregivers can't regulate their own emotional storms, their children tend to absorb the pattern and carry it forward, often without either generation quite realizing it's happening. I recently wrote that a relationship with no visible conflict often isn't a healthy one. The same is true of a household that looks calm on the surface while members inside it are either exploding, imploding, or quietly shutting down the moment discomfort arrives.

Those are not five different problems. They are the same untaught skill showing up in five distinct, perilous costumes. Taking emotional regulation seriously means people can disagree without dehumanizing each other. It means accountability without violence and conflict without catastrophe. None of that happens by accident. It is built moment by moment, usually starting with a single relationship willing to slow down.

If you want the healthiest, most resilient family, workplace, neighborhood, town, country, and world, it starts with teaching people how to feel and what to do with what they feel.
